To: Shared/Ops & HR
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: DRAFT: Brian’s Monday briefing — casuals’ pay and Kisumu loading

Brian,

I know you’ll be there at 5:30 and will have to face the guys without me. Thank you for taking this on. Please read this as your Sunday briefing, not as a script you have to deliver word for word. The main thing is to be straight with them, listen, and not promise a time we cannot keep.

This is our mess, not theirs. They did nothing wrong by expecting their Friday pay. Please go in with that in mind, not on the defensive.

What happened and where pay stands

The bank rejected Friday’s bulk payment file for all 212 casuals. A beneficiary reference field was too long under the bank’s new template, introduced after its platform upgrade. No payments in that file were processed.

Kevin only saw the rejection after 5pm because the alert went to the old finance mailbox. By then the bank’s cut-off had passed. Finance has taken responsibility for this.

Njeri has approved paying the affected list through M-Pesa bulk instead. Kevin’s realistic expectation is that the money will be on phones by 11am Monday. Please describe that as the expected time, not a guarantee. I would rather the guys hear an honest update than another deadline we then miss.

Njeri has also approved KES 500 per person for Monday lunch and fare for every casual on the affected list, to be paid in the same M-Pesa batch. The company is covering the M-Pesa charges; they are not to be deducted from anyone’s pay.

Peninah has confirmed 198 numbers. She could not reach 14 people, mostly new loaders from the Athi River intake. She will be at Embakasi from 7:30am with the list so they can give her their correct numbers face to face. She will also have her laptop for anyone who wants a printed payslip. Please don’t tell those 14 that their individual payments are certain to arrive by 11: their numbers still need to be checked, and we do not yet know whether that will affect their timing.

Before you address the group

Please find Ouma first and speak to him privately, before the whole group gathers. He is loud, but he is not a bad man. He has four children and rent to think about, and he is speaking from a real problem we caused. Ask him what he and the others need to know, hear him out, and explain the position honestly. Don’t make a separate bargain with him or ask him to silence the others. Then speak to everyone openly so nobody is left relying on rumours.

Joseph has heard that Ouma and two others are telling people not to load the Kisumu trucks until they see money. He also says people remember being told “tomorrow” for three days before. Expect them not to take our word easily. Give them room to ask questions, including the difficult ones.

What you can say

In your own words, I suggest:

“Management owes you an apology. Your Friday pay did not come through, and that is our mistake. The bank rejected our payment file, and none of the payments in it was processed. We should have picked it up sooner.

“We are arranging payment by M-Pesa. Finance expects the money to be on your phones by 11am today, but I won’t promise you an earlier time or pretend I can guarantee it. We have also approved KES 500 each for lunch and fare for everyone on the affected list, in the same batch, and the company will pay the M-Pesa charges.

“Peninah will be here from 7:30 with the list. Most numbers have been confirmed, but we still need to check 14. If yours is one of them, please see her so she can confirm the right number. She can also print your payslip if you want one.

“I know this delay has put people in a difficult position. I’ll listen to your questions, and I’ll give you the information I have rather than guess.”

Please make the apology in person, as Njeri asked. Don’t minimise the effect of the delay or tell people they should be satisfied with the extra KES 500. It is help with Monday’s lunch and fare, not a substitute for their wages.

What not to promise

No “by lunch,” no “in the next hour,” and no assurance that every phone will have money by a precise time. Remember Mombasa in 2024: the supervisor said “by lunch,” the money came at 4pm, and half the shift sat down. We must not repeat that.

Don’t say the payments have already been sent or processed unless Kevin confirms it. Don’t promise that a corrected number will be paid in a particular batch or at a particular time without checking with Finance. Don’t invent an answer if someone asks about their individual payment: take their details and get Peninah and Kevin to check.

And no threats about contracts or dismissal on Monday. That applies even if people refuse to load.

If Ouma’s group refuses to load

The Kisumu trucks need to leave by 9am to make the mill’s offloading slot, so we cannot wait until the expected 11am payment time to decide what to do. But the departure deadline does not change how we treat the team.

Keep the conversation calm and safe. Ask Ouma and the others what they are asking for, explain what we know and what we are checking, and listen without treating them as the problem. Let Joseph know what is happening, and involve HR alongside Operations immediately: the procedure is clear that a stoppage is handled jointly by Ops and HR, not by the supervisor alone. No one is to be dismissed or threatened with dismissal on the day.

Please contact me on WhatsApp if anything changes. I’ll be up from 4:30, and I need to hear from you before I board my 7:05 flight if there is a stoppage, a change to the payment position, or anything else material. If you cannot reach me after that, involve the available HR contact and keep Kevin informed on the payment questions. Please don’t leave the response waiting for my flight to land.

With the relevant Ops and HR people, establish whether loading can proceed safely and voluntarily and what the realistic departure position is. If the 9am departure is at risk, escalate that operational risk promptly through Ops and contact the mill about the offloading slot; don’t wait until 9 to raise it. Don’t pressure or threaten people into loading, and don’t make up a pay commitment to get the trucks out.

Keep a brief, factual record of what the group raises, who is involved in the response, what is communicated and when, and any operational decisions. Individual pay concerns can also go through Joseph and then HR under the grievance procedure; HR should receive grievances within 48 hours. A stoppage itself is handled jointly by Ops and HR.

Updates through the morning

Before speaking to the guys, check with Kevin for the latest on the M-Pesa batch. Give the group a clear next update time that you can actually meet, even if the update is simply that you are still waiting for confirmation. Once Peninah arrives, make sure the 14 people have a straightforward, private way to check their numbers with her. Don’t read phone numbers out to the group.

If the expected payment timing changes, tell people promptly and plainly: what has changed, what we know, what we don’t yet know, and when you will update them again. After payments are reported complete, ask Peninah and Kevin how individual missing payments should be checked and communicate that route to the team. Don’t assume a batch confirmation means every person has received theirs.

Thank you, Brian. I know this is a hard conversation to walk into on your own. Be honest with them, give them the apology they are owed, and keep me posted before I board.

Achieng
